Changes in the geographic range, abundance, and seasonal activity of vectors — such as mosquitoes, ticks and mites — that alter the transmission risk of vector-borne diseases.. Animal disease vectors also comprise other taxonomic groups than insects, e.g. ticks (mites, arachnids), other arthropods, and also mammals (e.g. bats, rats and mice). These changes have important implications for several diseases such as Chikungunya (vector: mosquitoes), dengue (vector: mosquitoes), encephalitis (e.g. tick-borne encephalitis, Japanese encephalitis, Murray Valley encephalitis, or West Nile encephalitis.), Hantavirus infection (vector: rodents), Lyme disease (vector: ticks), malaria (vector: mosquitoes), Rift Valley fever (vector: mosquitoes), West Nile virus infection (vector: mosquitoes), Zika virus infection (vector: mosquitoes), Ross River fever (vector: mosquitoes), Crimean-Congo haemorrhagic fever (vector: ticks), Leishmaniasis (vector: sandflies), Oropouche virus disease/fever (vector: midges, especially Culicoides paraensis).

In addition to releasing CO2, the burning or combustion of fossil fuels releases particulate air pollutants. 3. Household (indoor) air pollution (from combustion of fossil fuels used for cooking and heating) is a major contributor to ambient (outdoor) air pollution. Biomass burning (in agricultural production) also causes air pollution. 4. Include indoor air-pollution only if related to fossil fuel combustion. 5. Radon is considered an air quality related exposure which can occur indoor and outdoor (it is related to open mines and can be exacerbated by heat). 6. Metrics quantifying fatal health outcomes, including overall and cause-specific death rates across populations.

The rate at which new cases of a disease or condition occur in a defined population during a specified time period.

Uses a fixed reference age and measures years lost due to premature death.
A component of the Global Burden of Disease framework measuring the years of healthy life lost due to living with a non-fatal disease or disability, weighted by severity.
The rate of death from any cause within a defined population over a specified period, regardless of the underlying cause.

Measures quantifying the non-fatal impact of disease on individuals and populations, including disease frequency, duration, and effect on functional status and wellbeing.

A systematic review conducted within a shortened timeframe using streamlined methods, trading some comprehensiveness for speed to meet urgent policy or practice needs.

A time series analysis comparing outcome trends before and after an intervention or exposure in both an intervention group and a concurrent control group, strengthening causal inference over uncontrolled ITS.
